e.l: Do I need a permit for the peak?
e.a: 🌋 Yes. The final stretch, from La Rambleta to the crater (trail PNT 10 Telesforo Bravo), can only be walked with a prior authorisation, and going up without one can end in a fine. The permit is valid only for that stretch, that day and that time slot. Trails PNT 07 and PNT 09 need their own authorisation too.

e.l: Where do I book the permit?
e.a: 📅 On Tenerife ON (tenerifeon.es), the Cabildo’s official platform. You have to register first, it is free. Slots open every Monday at 07:00 Canary time for the following 56 days, and only one booking per person every 15 days is allowed. They go fast: be there first thing on Monday.

k: do i pay for the permit
e.a: 💶 It depends on the time slot. In the hours that match the cable car (9:00 to 17:00) there is a fee: residents in Tenerife and minors pay nothing, everyone else does, with one amount for residents elsewhere in the Canaries and another for the rest of visitors. Outside those hours there is no fee, but the booking is still compulsory. Tenerife ON shows you the exact amount as you book.

k: does the cable car reach the peak
how high does the cable car go
e.l: Does the cable car reach the peak?
e.a: ❌ No, and this is the costliest misunderstanding on the Teide. The ticket leaves you at La Rambleta, around 3,555 m; to carry on to the crater you need the PNT 10 permit, booked separately and not included. They are two independent things: in fact your permit is valid for its slot even if the cable car is not running that day.

e.l: How does the cable car work?
e.a: 🚡 It climbs from around 2,356 m to La Rambleta, about 3,555 m, in some eight minutes. Worth buying ahead because it sells out, and it closes with no warning in strong wind or ice. Check the day’s status on volcanoteide.com before driving up: it saves you a wasted trip.

🥾 Yes. You can reach La Rambleta on foot via Montaña Blanca (PNT 07), via Pico Viejo and Las Narices del Teide (PNT 09) or from Los Roques de García; the stratovolcano trails also require prior authorisation. And from there, the final stretch to the crater still needs the PNT 10 permit. Nothing is improvised here: it is all booked in advance.

⏱️ The final stretch is barely 0.66 km, but it takes close to an hour: it starts around 3,542 m, ends at 3,714 m and has slopes of up to 60 %. Officially it is medium difficulty, although at that altitude your body delivers half of what it normally does. Not suitable if you have heart, breathing or mobility problems.

e.l: Is there a park entrance fee?
e.a: 🎟️ No. The park is open: you can drive the road, stop at the viewpoints and walk most trails without paying anything. What has to be booked, and in some slots paid for, are the stratovolcano trails: PNT 10, PNT 07 and PNT 09. And note that smoking is banned in the park’s open spaces.

e.l: What should I wear? Is it cold?
e.a: 🧥 It is far colder up there than on the coast, and the peak trail has mandatory kit: proper mountain footwear, long trousers (worn or in your pack) and a fleece or warm layer. Without it, the control staff will not let you up. Add a hat, sunglasses, sunscreen, water and something to eat.

🫁 It can. At 3,700 m there is close to half the oxygen you get at sea level, and fatigue, headache and dizziness are normal, especially if you take the cable car and start walking right away. Go slowly, stop often, drink water and do not arrive on an empty stomach or hungover. If you really feel bad, go down.

❄️ It can snow in winter, and the Cabildo closes the park roads when there is ice: check road status before setting off. If there is snow or ice on the peak trail, the booking also demands crampons and an ice axe plus a declaration of high-mountain experience. Check the AEMET high-mountain forecast too, which is not the one for the village below.

e.l: Can I sleep in the refuge?
e.a: 🏔️ The Altavista refuge, at around 3,260 m, is the classic way to sleep up high and reach the summit early. Its opening, prices and booking method change with the season, so confirm on its website before building your plan around it. Sleeping rough inside the park is not allowed.

e.l: Where do I see the stars?
e.a: ✨ Las Cañadas has one of the best skies in Europe. To watch the stars on your own you need no permit: park at a viewpoint in the park, wrap up properly and wait for the valley lights to fade. Guided stargazing and visits to the Teide Observatory are booked separately. In the app, the 🔭 at the top tells you what you can see each night and where to go to watch.

👨‍👩‍👧 To the park and the cable car, yes, allowing for the cold and the altitude. To the peak trail, not entirely: under-3s are not allowed, and under-16s must always be accompanied by an adult. For them the La Rambleta viewpoints and the Los Roques de García walk usually work better.

📏 3,715 m: the highest point in Spain and the highest peak in the Atlantic. Measured from the ocean floor it goes beyond 7,000 m, which puts it among the tallest volcanoes in the world counting from its base.

e.l: Getting out of the South airport?
e.a: ✈️ From Tenerife South airport (TFS) there are direct buses: the 10 to Santa Cruz, the 40 express to Los Cristianos and Costa Adeje, and the 343 towards Puerto de la Cruz and the North airport. There are taxis at the door and private transfers too. You pay the driver in cash or by bank card; check the day’s timetable on titsa.com.

✈️ Tenerife North airport (TFN, Los Rodeos) is ten minutes from La Laguna. Airport express buses run to Santa Cruz and La Laguna, lines 20 and 30, and the 343 heads south and to Puerto de la Cruz. The tram does not enter the terminal, but it links La Laguna with Santa Cruz every few minutes.

k: how do i pay the bus
e.a: 🚌 The buses are run by TITSA and reach almost the whole island. You can pay the driver in cash with small notes, tap a contactless bank card on many routes, or use the ten+ card, which is noticeably cheaper on intercity journeys. I can tell you which line serves you and where the stop is; for the exact times of the day, titsa.com.

e.l: Is the ten+ card worth it?
e.a: 💳 The ten+ is the island’s transport card: you buy and top it up at stations, kiosks and machines, and there is a mobile version too. It pays off as soon as you make a few intercity journeys, because the discount against single tickets is large. You tap on boarding and, on long routes, when getting off as well.

e.l: Do I need a rental car?
e.a: 🚗 If you are going to stay around the coast and the towns, the bus covers it easily. If you want Anaga, Teno, the inland villages or a viewpoint at sunrise, rent one: there are places public transport barely reaches, and at awkward times. Plenty of people mix it: bus most days, car for two or three.

🛣️ Driving is fine, but the island is vertical: fast motorways on the coast, the TF-1 in the south and the TF-5 in the north, and mountain roads full of bends where 40 km can take well over an hour. Use low gears downhill, watch for cyclists and northern fog, and do not trust the time your sat nav gives you.

🅿️ In the cities there is paid blue-zone parking on weekdays and public car parks in the centre. In the well-known villages and viewpoints, arrive before ten or go at sunset: by mid-morning there is nothing left. Never park on a yellow line or on the bends by the viewpoints, the tow truck is quick.

⏱️ Rough guide, by car: Costa Adeje to Santa Cruz, a good hour on the motorway; Costa Adeje to the Teide, an hour and a half; Santa Cruz to Puerto de la Cruz, about 45 minutes; Santa Cruz to deep Anaga, an hour and a half even though it looks next door on the map. For the real route from where you are, tap «🚗 Get there by car» in any place’s pop-up: it opens in Google Maps or, on an iPhone, in Apple Maps.

🚋 The tram links Santa Cruz with La Laguna, line 1, and has a second route towards La Cuesta and Tíncer, line 2. It is the easiest way to move between the two cities and saves you the TF-5 jam. You pay with a ten+ card or a ticket from the platform machine, before boarding.

🚕 Taxis are white, metered, with airport and night surcharges; you take them at a rank, by phone or through your hotel, and in tourist areas there are ranks everywhere. Ride-hailing apps only work in some areas and with a small fleet, so do not count on them as plan A. For an excursion, agree a fixed price before getting in.

e.l: How do I reach another island?
e.a: ⛴️ Ferries to La Gomera leave from Los Cristianos, under an hour on the fast service, and there are sailings to La Palma and El Hierro too. For Gran Canaria you sail from Santa Cruz. Book online, and further ahead still if you are taking the car. Rough seas cancel crossings, so confirm before you set off.

e.l: Can I reach the Teide without a car?
e.a: 🚌🌋 Yes. Two tourist routes climb to the National Park: the 342 from Costa Adeje and the 348 from Puerto de la Cruz, with one morning departure and an afternoon return. Inside the park the 341 links Portillo, Montaña Blanca, the cable car and the Parador. Not every travel pass is valid on these routes, and you are tied to the single return: check the day’s timetable on titsa.com.

e.l: How do I get to Masca?
e.a: 🚌 To see the village, route 355 climbs up from Santiago del Teide and from Buenavista del Norte; parking up there is minimal, so the bus is the better idea anyway. For the gorge descent it is compulsory: you can only get in via the 355 transfer from Santiago del Teide, leaving the car at the cemetery car park, and arriving by private vehicle means you are not allowed to start.

k: is there a train in tenerife
e.l: Is there a train or metro?
e.a: 🚆 There is no train on Tenerife. The closest thing is the tram between Santa Cruz and La Laguna. For the rest of the island the bus network is the backbone, and for rural areas and odd hours, a car.

e.l: Can I rent a bike or scooter?
e.a: 🚲 Yes, you can rent bikes, e-bikes and scooters in the resort areas and at the harbours. The island is a serious road-cycling destination, with long climbs towards the Teide; for getting around town, the electric one earns its keep on the hills. Helmets are compulsory on a scooter, and on a bike outside built-up areas too.

e.l: Can I see the island in a day?
e.a: 🗺️ You can drive right round, but you end up seeing the viewpoints through the window. With one day, pick one axis: the Teide and Vilaflor, or Anaga and La Laguna, or the north coast from Garachico to Icod. Use the app’s planner to chain stops without overdoing the hours or the hairpins.

🛣️ No tolls: both motorways, the TF-1 in the south and the TF-5 in the north, are free. What does cost money is parking in town centres. And in high season the TF-1 clogs up around the south in the late afternoon, so leave a margin if you are heading to the airport.

🪪 With an EU licence you drive with no paperwork at all. If yours is from outside the EU, rental companies usually ask for an international permit alongside it, but each company sets its own rule: confirm with them before you fly, not at the desk on arrival.

⛽ Fuel is noticeably cheaper than on the mainland because the Canaries have their own tax regime. There are petrol stations all along the coast and in the midlands, but none inside the National Park or deep in Anaga: go up with a full tank. They are all on the map under their own category, and at the top, ⛽ uses your location to show the cheapest ones within 5, 10 or 20 km: petrol 95 and diesel, at the official price from the Spanish Ministry.

🏘️ The ones that never disappoint: La Orotava for its mansions and carved balconies, Garachico for the sea and the lava, La Laguna for the old town, Masca and Taganana for the landscape, Vilaflor for the altitude and Candelaria for the basilica facing the Atlantic. Tell me your area and I will sort them by distance.

e.l: What to see in La Laguna?
e.a: 🏛️ It is a World Heritage site: the first unwalled colonial city, with a layout later copied across the Americas. Wander on foot among mansions with inner courtyards, climb the Concepción tower and eat tapas along Calle Herradores and the market. From Santa Cruz the tram gets you there in twenty minutes.

e.l: What to see in La Orotava?
e.a: 🌺 The town of grand houses with pine-wood balconies and courtyards full of flowers. Do not miss the Casa de los Balcones, the Concepción church and the valley view from the Humboldt lookout. At Corpus Christi the streets are carpeted with flowers and sand from the Teide, and it is worth the trip.

⚓ It was the island’s great port until the 1706 eruption half buried it; out of that lava came the natural pools of El Caletón. Today it is a quiet town with the San Miguel castle, squares with a dragon tree and good swimming when the sea allows. A perfect half day, better on a weekday.

e.l: What to see in Santa Cruz?
e.a: 🏙️ The capital is far livelier than visitors expect: Calatrava’s Auditorio, the Plaza de España, the Nuestra Señora de África market, the TEA art centre, the Palmetum built on a former landfill, and Las Teresitas beach ten minutes away. Plus the best shopping on the island.

🎭 The one in Santa Cruz is among the biggest in the world: the Queen’s gala, murga choirs, comparsa dance troupes and whole nights of dancing in the street. It falls in February or March depending on Lent, so check the dates for the year. It ends with the Burial of the Sardine, and Puerto de la Cruz has its own version. If you are here, wear a costume: everyone does.

🎉 Every town has its patron saint and its romería, the festival in the saint’s honour, so there is nearly always something on. The big ones are Carnival, the Corpus Christi in La Orotava, the Virgin of Candelaria in August and San Andrés in late November, when the new wine is opened. Check the month’s listings in the app, they change every year.

🐂 It is a town’s festival in honour of its patron saint: ox-drawn carts, traditional dress, folk bands playing and neighbours handing out wine, potatoes and meat to whoever walks past. You do not pay and you do not need an invitation. You walk in, say hello and accept what you are offered, which is half the fun.

🗿 They were the island’s inhabitants before the Castilian conquest: shepherds of Berber origin who lived in caves, organised themselves into menceyatos (kingdoms) and mummified their dead. Tenerife was the last island to fall, in 1496. To see it up close, the Museum of Nature and Archaeology in Santa Cruz keeps the mummies.

🖼️ The essentials: the Museum of Nature and Archaeology for the Guanche mummies, the TEA for contemporary art, the Casa del Vino in El Sauzal and the History Museum in La Laguna. Opening hours and free-entry days change often, so confirm them before turning up.

🧺 The farmers’ markets are the best weekend stop: Tacoronte, La Laguna, Güímar or the Nuestra Señora de África market in Santa Cruz, which opens daily. Days and hours vary by municipality, so confirm before setting off. Go early and take cash.

🐬 There are resident pilot whales and bottlenose dolphins all year in the sea strip between Teno and Rasca, one of the best places in the world to see them. Boats leave from Los Cristianos, Puerto Colón and Los Gigantes. Pick an operator with the Barco Azul mark, which certifies respectful watching, and do not get in the water with them.

e.l: What if I only have one day?
e.a: 🗓️ I would drive up to the Teide early via Vilaflor, have lunch around La Orotava and drop down to Garachico or Puerto de la Cruz at sunset. It makes a complete day and you get three different islands in one: the volcanic summit, the green valley and the north coast. I can chain the stops in the planner for you.

🗺️ With three days: the Teide, Anaga and a day on the south coast. With five, add Teno with Masca and Garachico, plus a day on the northern beaches. With seven, fit in La Gomera by ferry and one unplanned day in La Laguna or Santa Cruz. Save the places to favourites and I will sort them by distance so you do not cross the island twice.

e.l: Is La Gomera worth a day trip?
e.a: ⛴️ Worth it if you get up early: in under an hour you are in San Sebastián, with time to go up to the Garajonay National Park, eat in a village in the north and come back in the afternoon. Book the return for the same day and bear in mind that rough seas cancel crossings: if being stranded would ruin things, sleep over instead.

e.l: Where can I dive or snorkel?
e.a: 🤿 The dive centres cluster in the south, with mild water all year and good visibility: around Las Galletas, Los Cristianos and Radazul. For snorkelling without tanks, the natural pools at low tide and the sheltered coves of the south. In the north the sea calls the shots far more than it looks from the shore.

🪂 The island is excellent for flying, with classic launch sites above the Orotava valley and around Adeje. You fly tandem with a pilot, so no experience is needed. The flight depends on the day’s wind: book with some slack and expect them to move your time or your launch site.

e.l: Where can I kayak or paddleboard?
e.a: 🛶 In the south, where the sea is calmest: Los Cristianos, Playa Paraíso, Los Gigantes and the Adeje coast, where you can easily run into turtles. You rent by the hour or go with a guide, who will also take you into the coastal caves. In the north, only with a flat sea and only if you know what you are doing.

🌙 Depends what you are after. Las Américas and Costa Adeje hold the tourist nightlife, with clubs and bars running late. Santa Cruz and La Laguna have the local scene, with the bar district downtown and terraces full of people. People go out late here: at weekends things get going from midnight onwards.

⛳ There are about a dozen courses, most in the south and a few in the north with views of the Teide and the sea. You can play all year, which is exactly why people come in winter. In the hotter months, book an early tee time. They are on the map under their own category, with directions.

e.l: What is there to do on a Sunday?
e.a: ☀️ On Sunday the island heads for the countryside: recreation areas with barbecues, packed guachinches, a romería (a patron-saint festival) if one falls that weekend and farmers markets in the morning. Many shops close, but restaurants, beaches and trails are at their best. It is the best day to see the island in local mode, and the worst for shopping.

🚌 Perfectly possible. Buses reach the Teide, Masca, Anaga and nearly every village, and from the south there are organised excursions that pick you up at your hotel. What changes is the rhythm: you are tied to the return timetable, so check the last departure before you set off and do not cut it fine.

💶 The euro. You can pay by card almost everywhere, even for small amounts. Still carry some cash for guachinches, street markets, village car parks and the odd taxi. Cash machines are easy to find, but watch the fees on the ones in tourist areas.

e.l: Can I drink the tap water?
e.a: 🚰 It is drinkable and monitored, but since much of it is desalinated or heavily mineralised, the taste puts people off and almost everyone, locals included, drinks bottled. For cooking and washing it is perfectly fine. On hikes, only refill at springs marked as drinkable.

🔌 The European two-round-pin ones, types C and F, at 230 volts and 50 hertz. Coming from the UK, Ireland or outside Europe, bring an adapter: you can buy one at the airport or in supermarkets, but it costs more. Modern chargers handle the voltage without a transformer.

🛂 The Canaries are Spain and Schengen territory: coming from the European Union, an ID card or passport is enough and there is no border check. From outside, a passport and, depending on your nationality, a visa or prior authorisation. Requirements change, so confirm them with a Spanish consulate before you fly.

🕐 The Canaries run one hour behind mainland Spain and central Europe, and match the UK and Portugal. The clock change happens at the same time as in the rest of the European Union. It is the detail that catches people out on arrival: if you flew from Madrid, put your watch back.

🗣️ No problem. The language is Spanish, but English is widespread in the resort areas and you will hear plenty of German in the north too. Inland it thins out, though gestures and a friendly face solve everything. People here help before you even ask.

🗨️ The ones you will hear most: guagua is the bus, papas are potatoes, cotufas are popcorn, millo is sweetcorn, un fisco means a tiny bit, and you already know guachinche. You will also notice people use «ustedes» where mainland Spain says «vosotros», and nobody pronounces the final s.

e.l: Is there wifi? Do I need an eSIM?
e.a: 📶 Wifi is available in accommodation, bars and many public spaces. Mobile coverage is good all along the coast and in the towns, and non-existent at the bottom of the ravines and in parts of Anaga and Teno. From the European Union you use your own data at no extra cost; otherwise a local eSIM is worth it.

🧳 Summer clothes for the coast, comfortable shoes with grip, swimwear and high-factor sun cream. Add a light jacket for the evenings and something properly warm if you are going up the Teide, even in August. If you plan to walk, bring mountain footwear; flip-flops are no use on the trails.

k: how many days do i need
e.l: How many days do I need?
e.a: 📆 A week is ideal and lets you see the island without rushing. Five days works well if you avoid wasting time crossing from end to end. With three you are tight: pick two areas and forget the rest. Less than that is a stopover, not a trip.

🕙 Small shops usually open in the morning, close at midday and reopen in the afternoon; shopping centres and large stores stay open all day. Many shops close on Sundays, except in the resort areas. Hours vary by season and by municipality, so check before you drive across the island.

🧾 It is the Canaries’ own indirect tax, replacing VAT and noticeably lower. That is why electronics, perfume, tobacco and spirits come out cheaper than on the mainland. Refund conditions for travellers change, so ask in the shop as you pay and keep the receipt.

💰 Cheaper than most European sun destinations, largely because the IGIC is lower than mainland VAT. What pushes the spend up is the area: the tourist seafront and the theme parks. Away from those, eating, getting around by bus and the beach are inexpensive, and the landscape costs nothing.

ℹ️ Tenerife GO in a nutshell:
• The map: tap a marker to see what it is, its opening hours if it has them and how to get there by car or bus; on the coast, the sea conditions too
• At the top: the dice 🎲, the cheapest petrol station near you ⛽, the map layers, the weather by area, the sea, the fiestas, the night sky 🔭, the buses and the language
• On the sides: search 🔍 and the categories
• At the bottom: Favorites, Routes, this Assistant and your Account
• The app tour is always in the map legend: «Take the tour»
Ask me about any feature and I will explain it.

e.l: How do I save a place to favourites?
e.a: ⭐ In the pop-up of any place, tap «Add to favourites». At the bottom, Favorites shows only the places you have saved on the map, with a counter. Without an account they stay on this phone; if you sign in, they are also saved in the cloud and you have them on any device.

e.l: How do I mark a place as visited?
e.a: ✅ In the pop-up of every place there is «○ Mark visited»: tap it and it turns into «✓ Visited». It counts towards your achievements 🏆 and is saved on this phone.

🏆 You unlock achievements by marking places as visited: the more you mark, the more you earn, and there is a special one for the summit of the Teide. Tap the trophy 🏆 on the right of the map to see the ones you have and how many places you have visited.

e.l: Can I listen to a place’s description?
e.a: 🔊 Yes. In the pop-up of every place, «▶ Listen» reads out the name and the description, in the language you have set and with your phone’s voice. If your phone has no voice for that language, the button does not appear; if you hear nothing, turn the volume up.

📴 Yes, once you have opened it with a connection. With no signal, the places and their details, search, the categories, the buses with their stops, the night sky 🔭 and this assistant all keep working. In the map layers you have «Island offline», a map of the whole island that comes inside the app; «Satellite» and «Topo» also keep the areas you have already looked at. Live things do need a connection: the weather, the sea conditions, the cloud forecast for the night sky, the car route and the webcams.

e.l: How do I install the app?
e.a:
📲 It is not in the app stores: you install it from the browser.
• iPhone: in Safari, tap the Share button (square with arrow) and choose «Add to Home Screen»
• Android: in Chrome, open the ⋮ menu and choose «Install app»
It then sits on your home screen like any other app.

e.l: How do I change the language?
e.a: 🌐 Tap the flag, the last button on the top bar, and pick your language: the app comes in {L} languages. The interface, the details of the {N} places, the «Listen» voice and my answers all change.

e.l: How do I search for a place?
e.a: 🔍 Tap the magnifying glass on the left of the map and type the name of the place or a category, with or without accents. As you type, suggestions appear and the map keeps only what matches; if you press Enter and there is a single result, it takes you there and opens its pop-up. The ✕ clears it. You can also ask me: «where is the Drago Milenario?».

e.l: How do I filter by category?
e.a: 🗂️ The categories button on the right of the map opens the filters in tabs: nature and beaches, culture, sport, viewpoints, markets… and also pet-friendly or accessible places. Each category shows how many places it has. Tap several and the map shows only those; press and hold one to keep just that one. «Show all» removes the filter. You can also ask me: «viewpoints».
🎲 It takes you to a random place and opens its pop-up. If you have categories selected, the surprise comes from them: with «Viewpoints» on, you get a viewpoint.

e.l: What do I see when I tap a place?
e.a: 📍 Tapping a marker opens its pop-up: what it is and its description in your language, opening hours and phone number if it has them, safety notes ⚠️ if there are any and, on the coast, the sea conditions. Below are «Add to favourites», «Share», «▶ Listen», «○ Mark visited», «🚏 How to get there by bus» and «🚗 Get there by car». «See full description» opens the complete details.

e.l: Where can I see today’s weather?
e.a: 🌡️ At the top, the thermometer gives you the live weather, area by area: here it can rain in one village and be sunny in the next. The wave 🌊 shows the sea conditions by coast and, in «Swim here today», up to three beaches based on the current sea and wind; the pop-up of every coastal place has the sea right there. If AEMET has warnings in force for Tenerife, the wave has a yellow, orange or red dot and, when you open it, they come first: tap one to read it in full. If the warning is for coastal events, «Swim here today» leaves out the beaches on that coast. It needs a connection.

e.l: What are the ⚠️ notes on some places?
e.a: ⚠️ Some places carry their own safety note in their pop-up: rough sea and currents, high mountain, demanding route, unfenced edges, forest area with fire risk or narrow mountain road. Read it before you go.

e.l: How do I plan a route from A to B?
e.a: 🧭 In Routes, at the bottom, «A→B» tab: choose the start and the destination by tapping the map, typing an address or using GPS, and press «Calculate route». It gives you the minutes and kilometres by car and the bus options. To drive to a specific place, its pop-up has «🚗 Get there by car».

e.l: Can you help me plan my day?
e.a: ✨ In Routes, at the bottom, «Plan your day» tab: say how much time you have, what you fancy (nature, beach, culture, food… one or several), whether you prefer the north or the south (or don’t mind) and how you are getting around (car, bus, on foot or bike), and it puts together an itinerary. You can redo it, save it to «Day Route» or to Favorites, and share it.

k: how to get there by bus
e.l: Which bus takes me to a place?
e.a: 🚏 In the pop-up of every place, «🚏 How to get there by bus» shows the stops closest to it and the lines that call at each one. Tap a stop to see its line on the map. Times for the day are on titsa.com.

👤 No: the app is the same without an account. In Account, at the bottom, you can «Continue as guest». If you sign up with email and password, your favourites are also saved in the cloud and you get them back on another device; without an account they stay on this phone.

e.l: How do I share a place?
e.a: 📤 In the pop-up of every place, tap «Share»: your phone’s share menu opens (WhatsApp, email…). If your phone does not have one, the text with the link is copied and you get a notice.
📖 In the fiestas panel 🎉 at the top, the «📚 Speak like a Canarian» button opens up local words with their meaning: guagua, chacho, ños, papas arrugadas, mojo, guachinche…

e.l: What do I do if something fails?
e.a:
🔧 Try this:
1. Close the app and open it again, or reload the page
2. If it was something live (the weather, the sea, a route), check that you have a connection

🛍️ The shop is not available for now. If you have a business in Tenerife and would like to appear in the app, write to tenerife.go.app@gmail.com.

📍 Ask me like this: «sort my favourites by distance». I put them in order from where you are and without going back and forth, so you do not cross the island twice. If you do not let me know where you are, I start from the one at one end. The distances are in a straight line, not by road.

e.l: What can I see in the sky tonight?
e.a: 🔭 At the top, the telescope opens «Tenerife night sky». In «Tonight» you get when full darkness begins, the Moon, the planets you can see and whether the Milky Way rises, with the cloud forecast; in «Calendar», the coming meteor showers and eclipses; in «Catalog», stars, clusters and galaxies by whether you see them with the naked eye, binoculars or a telescope; in «Sky map», the sky at the time you choose; and in «Where to go», the places to watch from. It is calculated on your phone and works offline, except the clouds. «Red light» tints the screen so it does not dazzle you.

e.l: When are the meteor showers and eclipses?
e.a: 📅 In the 🔭 at the top, «Calendar» tab: the meteor showers with the night of their peak and how the Moon will be, and the solar and lunar eclipses with what will be visible from Tenerife and at what time. It is calculated for Izaña, in Canary Islands time. For a solar eclipse, never without certified ISO 12312-2 glasses or a solar filter in front of the lens.

e.l: How do I delete my account?
e.a: 🗑️ In «Account», at the bottom, signed in: below «Log out», tap «Delete account» and confirm with «Yes, delete my account». Your email address, your password and the favourites saved in the cloud are deleted, and it cannot be undone. If you cannot do it from the app, write to tenerife.go.app@gmail.com from your account’s email address with the subject «Delete my account»: it is deleted within one month at the latest. Notifications are not part of the account: you turn them off in your browser or in your phone’s settings.

e.l: What data does the app keep?
e.a: 🔒 It is all in «Privacy · GDPR», at the bottom of the map, and on the web in «Web version». Your location, only when you turn it on, and it is not stored on any server; your email address and password, if you create an account; your favourites, in the cloud only with an account; and, if you turn on notifications, your browser’s subscription. Usage statistics, only if you accept the cookie notice. To delete your account, «Delete your account», right next to it.

💼 They are businesses that pay a monthly promotion plan to appear on the map: their pop-up says so, «Sponsored». Everyone sees them the same way, without using your data or advertising cookies, and they do not change the rest of the content.

e.l: Can I get a message every morning?
e.a: 🔔 Yes, with the app installed on your home screen: the third time you open it, it asks «A little nudge each morning?», a line to start the day, with no ads. If you answered «Not now», it does not ask again, but you can turn them on whenever you like in «Account», with «Turn on notifications»: signed in, right there; without an account, under «Continue as guest». On iPhone, first add it to your home screen from Safari. To stop them, go to your phone’s notification settings.

e.l: What number do I call in an emergency?
e.a: 🚨 For any emergency, call 112: it is free, works 24 hours a day and they answer in Spanish, English and German. If you are in the mountains or on the coast, say where you are as precisely as you can: the name of the trail or the beach and something you can see nearby.

🌊 Here the Atlantic is in charge. Always check the flag: green, safe to swim; yellow, swim with caution; red, no swimming. The others are in the pop-up of every beach, under «What does each flag mean?». Where there is no lifeguard, take extra care, and in rough seas stay away from the edge of rocks and rock pools. If a current pulls you, do not swim against it: swim parallel to the shore or float, and call for help by waving your arms. Emergencies: 112.

🌫️ Calima is Saharan dust hanging in the air: the sky turns yellowish and air quality gets worse. The Canary Islands Health Department advises drinking water, avoiding physical effort outdoors, not spending long outside and keeping windows closed; if you have asthma or another respiratory or heart condition, and with children and older people, take extra care. If AEMET issues a suspended dust warning, you see it in the app: a coloured dot on the wave 🌊 and the warning at the very top when you open it. Also on the AEMET website.

e.l: What precautions should I take in the mountains?
e.a: 🥾 In the mountains the weather changes fast with altitude. Take plenty of water, a cap, sun protection and something warm; tell someone your route and when you plan to be back; stay on the marked trail and do not go into a ravine if it is raining or about to rain. Before you set off, read the ⚠️ note in the pop-up if there is one and check closures and bookings on tenerifeon.es. If something happens: 112.

e.l: How do I protect myself from the sun?
e.a: ☀️ The Canary Islands have the highest ultraviolet levels in Spain all year round, and clouds do not stop them. The Canary Islands Public Health Department advises SPF 30 or higher (50 or higher when the index is very high), shade, a hat, covering clothes and sunglasses. On the Teide, with the altitude, the sun is even stronger. If someone feels unwell from the heat, get them into the shade and give them water; if it is serious, 112. The UV forecast for each island is on the AEMET website.

💊 Pharmacies have a green cross, and in every area there is always one on duty, on a rota that changes every day. On the map they are in the Pharmacies category, and the pop-up of each one has the «💊 Find today's on-duty pharmacy» link. For an emergency, 112.

e.l: What if I need a doctor?
e.a: 🏥 If you come from the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland or the United Kingdom, the European Health Insurance Card gives you the necessary medical care in the public health system, on the same terms as residents. It does not cover private care or repatriation, so travel insurance is still a good idea; if you come from another country, get one. The map shows the hospitals with 24-hour emergency departments and the health centres. If it is serious, 112.

e.l: Where can I get help if I suffer violence?
e.a: 🆘 If you are in danger, call 112. 016 helps women 24 hours a day. In Tenerife, the 24-hour Crisis Centre for victims of sexual violence helps women over 16, free of charge and confidentially, also without reporting it, and the Cabildo’s SIAM gives psychological, legal and social support to women who are victims of gender violence, by appointment. You have them on the map, in the «Help & Support» category.

🍽️ What you cannot leave without trying: papas arrugadas with red and green mojo, gofio, local cheese, fresh fish, goat meat and conejo en salmorejo (rabbit in a spicy marinade), and for dessert bienmesabe or quesillo. To drink, local wine or a barraquito. On the map, the Gastronomy category.

🍷 A guachinche is a place where the winegrower sells wine from their own harvest, along with a few traditional dishes. The Canary Islands Government regulates them: they can only open for a few months a year and close when the wine runs out, so the one you liked may not be open. On the map they are under Gastronomy, and most of them are in the north.

e.l: What are papas arrugadas with mojo?
e.a: 🥔 Small potatoes boiled with lots of salt until the skin wrinkles; you eat them skin and all, dipped in mojo: the red one, or picón, made with peppers, and the green one, with coriander. It is the Canarian dish par excellence.
🌾 Gofio is flour made from toasted cereals, and the ancient Canarians already ate it. It is eaten savoury, in escaldón (mixed with broth), and sweet, in milk or in desserts.
☕ The island’s coffee, served in a glass in layers: condensed milk, liqueur, coffee, frothed milk, cinnamon and lemon peel. If you do not want alcohol, ask for it without liqueur.

e.l: What wine is made in Tenerife?
e.a: 🍇 Tenerife has five designations of origin of its own: Abona, Tacoronte-Acentejo, Valle de Güímar, Valle de La Orotava and Ycoden-Daute-Isora. The Casa del Vino in El Sauzal brings them all together and is a good place to start. And at San Andrés, at the end of November, the new wine is opened.
🧀 Goat’s cheese rules on the island: fresh, semi-cured, cured or smoked. You will see it grilled with mojo or with palm honey. Local cheeses are sold at the farmers’ markets.

e.l: What is the weather like in Tenerife?
e.a: 🌤️ An island of microclimates: the trade winds leave more cloud and more green in the north, while the south and west are drier and sunnier. In summer the low morning clouds of the «panza de burro» are typical in the north; on the summit it is properly cold and in winter it can snow. If it is cloudy where you are, crossing the island often changes that. For today’s weather, area by area, use the thermometer 🌡️ at the top.

e.l: When is the best time to come?
e.a: 📅 Any time: on the coast the climate is mild all year. What changes is the plan: in summer, more heat and warmer sea; in winter, possible snow on the Teide; in February or March, Carnival. If you want to climb to the Teide peak, check early that there are permit places.

e.l: Should I stay in the north or the south?
e.a: 🧭 It depends on what you are after. The south (Costa Adeje, Los Cristianos, El Médano) has the most reliable sun and the easiest beaches. The north (Puerto de la Cruz, La Orotava, Garachico) is greener and more Canarian, with the guachinches close by. The island is not big: wherever you sleep, the other side is a day trip away.

🏖️ There are beaches of black volcanic sand, golden sand and pebbles, and they are very different depending on the coast: in the south, more sheltered and with facilities; in the north and in Anaga, wilder and with bigger waves. Before swimming, check each beach’s pop-up for its ⚠️ note if it has one, the flag and the sea conditions.

💧 They are seawater pools among the lava, almost all on the north coast. Swim only when the sea is calm, get in by the steps and wear water shoes, because the rock is sharp. In rough seas, stay away from the edge. Each pool’s pop-up has its safety note and the sea conditions.

e.l: What can I do with kids?
e.a: 👨‍👩‍👧 The map has the Family and Animals categories: water parks and animal parks, hands-on museums, beaches with calm water… They can go up the Teide by cable car, bearing in mind the cold and the altitude. And in Routes, «Plan your day», choose Family and the app puts the plan together.

k: what to do if it rains
e.l: What can I do if it rains?
e.a: 🌧️ First, cross the island: if it rains in the north, the south is usually sunny. If you would rather be indoors, go for museums: the Museum of Nature and Archaeology in Santa Cruz or the Museum of Science and the Cosmos in La Laguna. The Cueva del Viento lava tube in Icod is visited by booking. On the map, the Museums category.

e.l: What can I do for free?
e.a: 🆓 Plenty: the beaches, the viewpoints, the old towns of La Laguna, La Orotava or Garachico, the markets and most trails, including those in Teide National Park, which has no entrance fee. Some trails need booking in advance even though they are free, like the Bosque Encantado in Anaga; the Teide peak trail also needs an authorisation.

🥾 To start with: the Sendero de los Sentidos at Cruz del Carmen (Anaga), with short loops and one adapted for wheelchairs; the Roques de García loop in Teide National Park; and the coastal walk from Almáciga to Roque de las Bodegas, also in Anaga. Tap each one on the map to see its details.

🚁 Very carefully: in Teide National Park and the other protected natural areas you cannot fly a drone for leisure without authorisation, and the Guardia Civil issues fines. For everything else, check the AESA rules (aesa.gob.es) before take-off: registration, insurance and no-fly zones, such as near airports.

🏕️ Only in authorised areas: camping outside them is forbidden and fined. The Cabildo has camping areas in the hills, free with prior authorisation. On the map they are in the Campsites category. They can close when there is a fire risk, so check their status before you go.

🚌 The 111 links the Santa Cruz Intercambiador with the Costa Adeje bus station, by way of Los Cristianos. At the top, in the buses button 🚌, search for it by its number and tap it: it is drawn on the map with all its stops. The day’s times are on titsa.com.

e.l: What should I know about the Teide?
e.a: 🌋 At 3,715 m the Teide is the highest point in Spain, and entry to the National Park is free. The cable car goes up to La Rambleta, at about 3,555 m, with no permit; the last stretch to the crater needs a prior authorisation, booked on Tenerife ON and not included in the ticket. Up there it is cold and there is less oxygen: wrap up and go slowly. Without a car, buses 342 and 348 get you there.

🌿 Anaga Rural Park, in the north-east, is a Biosphere Reserve covered in laurel forest. To start, the Cruz del Carmen Visitor Centre and the Sendero de los Sentidos; then the hamlets and wild beaches of Taganana, Benijo and Almáciga. The Bosque Encantado (El Pijaral) can only be visited with a free prior permit: details in its entry. It is often misty and the ground is slippery: wear good shoes.

e.l: How do I get to Punta de Teno?
e.a: 🌅 Punta de Teno is the island’s north-western tip, with its lighthouse and views of La Gomera. The last stretch of road is regulated: during the regulated hours you cannot drive up in a private car, and you go on the shuttle bus from Buenavista del Norte. Check the current times before you go.

e.l: What is the Barranco del Infierno like?
e.a: 💦 It is a trail in Adeje that goes up the ravine to a waterfall, in a protected area with a limited number of visitors per day. Booking is compulsory at barrancodelinfierno.es; so is the helmet, which they give you there. It closes on rainy or windy days. Take water and hiking shoes.
